prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The presence of dust at high redshift requires efficient condensation of grains in SN ejecta, in accordance with current theoretical models. Yet, observations of the few well studied SNe and SN remnants imply condensation efficiencies which are about two orders of magnitude smaller. Motivated by this tension, we have (i) revisited the model of Todini & Ferrara (2001) for dust formation in the ejecta of core collapse SNe and (ii) followed, for the first time, the evolution of newly condensed grains from the time of formation to their survival - through the passage of the reverse shock - in the SN remnant. We find that 0.1 - 0.6 M_sun of dust form in the ejecta of 12 - 40 M_sun stellar progenitors. Depending on the density of the surrounding ISM, between 2-20% of the initial dust mass survives the passage of the reverse shock, on time-scales of about 4-8 x 10^4 yr from the stellar explosion. Sputtering by the hot gas induces a shift of the dust size distribution towards smaller grains. The resulting dust extinction curve shows a good agreement with that derived by observations of a reddened QSO at z =6.2. Stochastic heating of small grains leads to a wide distribution of dust temperatures. This supports the idea that large amounts (~ 0.1 M_sun) of cold dust (T ~ 40K) can be present in SN remnants, without being in conflict with the observed IR emission.

outputs.L1: The presence of dust at high redshift requires efficient grain condensation in supernova (SN) ejecta, consistent with current theoretical models. However, observations of the few well-studied SNe and SN remnants suggest condensation efficiencies approximately two orders of magnitude lower. Motivated by this discrepancy, we have (i) revisited the dust-formation model of Todini & Ferrara (2001) for the ejecta of core-collapse SNe and (ii) followed, for the first time, the evolution of newly condensed grains from their formation through the passage of the reverse shock to their survival in the SN remnant. We find that \(0.1\text{–}0.6\,M_\odot\) of dust forms in the ejecta of \(12\text{–}40\,M_\odot\) stellar progenitors. Depending on the density of the surrounding interstellar medium, \(2\text{–}20\%\) of the initial dust mass survives the passage of the reverse shock over timescales of approximately \(4\text{–}8 \times 10^4\) yr after the stellar explosion. Sputtering by the hot gas shifts the dust-size distribution toward smaller grains. The resulting dust-extinction curve agrees well with that inferred from observations of a reddened QSO at \(z=6.2\). Stochastic heating of small grains produces a broad distribution of dust temperatures, supporting the possibility that large amounts (\(\sim 0.1\,M_\odot\)) of cold dust (\(T\sim40\) K) may be present in SN remnants without conflicting with the observed infrared emission.
outputs.L2:
The detection of dust at high redshift suggests that grains must condense efficiently within supernova (SN) ejecta, as predicted by current theoretical models. However, measurements of the limited number of well-studied SNe and SN remnants indicate efficiencies roughly 100 times lower. To investigate this discrepancy, we re-examined the core-collapse SN dust-formation model developed by Todini & Ferrara (2001). We also tracked, for the first time, newly formed grains from their initial condensation through their interaction with the reverse shock to determine their survival within the remnant.

Our results indicate that ejecta from stellar progenitors of 12–40 M_sun produce approximately 0.1–0.6 M_sun of dust. Depending on the density of the ambient interstellar medium (ISM), about 2–20% of this original dust mass remains after the reverse shock passes, approximately 4–8 × 10^4 years after the explosion. Sputtering in the hot gas alters the grain-size distribution by favoring smaller particles. The corresponding extinction curve closely matches that inferred from observations of a reddened quasar at z = 6.2. In addition, stochastic heating produces a broad range of temperatures among small grains. This finding supports the possibility that SN remnants contain substantial quantities—around 0.1 M_sun—of cold dust at roughly 40 K without contradicting the observed infrared emission.
outputs.L3:
The presence of substantial quantities of dust at high redshift implies that dust grains must condense efficiently in supernova ejecta, because lower-mass stellar sources may not have had sufficient time to contribute. Observationally inferred condensation efficiencies, however, are typically about two orders of magnitude lower than theoretical predictions, creating an apparent tension between models and measurements.

Revised calculations suggest that core-collapse supernovae with progenitor masses of approximately 12–40 solar masses can initially form about 0.1–0.6 solar masses of dust in their ejecta. Much of this newly formed material is subsequently processed by the reverse shock as the expanding ejecta interact with the surrounding interstellar medium. The survival fraction depends strongly on the ambient gas density: after roughly 40,000–80,000 years, only about 2–20% of the original dust mass may remain.

Shock-driven sputtering also modifies the grain-size distribution by eroding grains and shifting it toward smaller sizes. The resulting wavelength-dependent extinction can reproduce the unusual extinction curve observed toward a reddened quasar at a redshift of 6.2, supporting the idea that supernova-produced dust contributed to extinction in the early universe.

Finally, dust temperatures in supernova remnants cannot always be represented by a single equilibrium value. Stochastic heating—especially important for small grains—produces a broad distribution of grain temperatures and infrared emission. When this effect is included, a remnant can contain approximately 0.1 solar masses of relatively cold dust at about 40 K without exceeding or otherwise conflicting with the observed infrared emission. Together, these results indicate that supernovae can be important early dust producers, although reverse-shock destruction substantially reduces the amount of dust ultimately injected into the interstellar medium.
outputs.L4:
Large quantities of dust have been detected in galaxies and quasars at high redshift, when the Universe was still too young for low-mass, evolved stars to have produced most of the observed material. Core-collapse supernovae are therefore often proposed as rapid sources of cosmic dust. This interpretation, however, has been challenged by the relatively low dust-condensation efficiencies inferred from observations of many young supernovae. An additional uncertainty is that newly formed grains may subsequently be heated, sputtered, or destroyed when the reverse shock propagates through the expanding ejecta.

To investigate whether supernovae can nevertheless account for the early dust budget, a core-collapse supernova dust-formation model was revisited and coupled to calculations of grain evolution within the supernova remnant. The model follows dust condensation in the cooling ejecta and then tracks the resulting grain populations as they encounter the reverse shock. Grain heating, erosion, and destruction are considered over tens of thousands of years, allowing the amount and composition of surviving dust to be estimated rather than equating the initial condensation yield with the material ultimately injected into the surrounding medium.

The calculations indicate that a single core-collapse supernova can initially form approximately 0.1–0.6 solar masses of dust, depending on the progenitor and ejecta conditions. Reverse-shock processing destroys a large fraction of this material, but does not eliminate it completely. After roughly 40,000–80,000 years, about 2–20% of the newly condensed dust is predicted to survive. The surviving fraction is strongly influenced by grain size and composition, because larger and more resistant grains are less vulnerable to sputtering and other destructive processes.

The modeled grain populations also produce extinction curves and infrared-emission characteristics broadly consistent with those inferred from high-redshift quasars. These results help reconcile the substantial dust masses observed in the early Universe with the modest condensation efficiencies derived from observations of young supernovae. They further suggest that supernova remnants may contain significant reservoirs of cold dust that are difficult to detect at shorter wavelengths. Consequently, core-collapse supernovae remain plausible and potentially important contributors to the rapid enrichment of early galaxies with dust, even after reverse-shock destruction is taken into account.
outputs.L5:
The night sky often appears calm and unchanging, yet it is filled with powerful cosmic events. Among the most spectacular are supernovae, commonly abbreviated as SNe. These stellar explosions occur when certain stars reach the end of their lives, releasing enormous amounts of energy and scattering heavy elements into space.

Although SNe are relatively rare in individual galaxies, they are essential to the evolution of the universe. The material produced by these explosions can eventually become part of new stars, planets, and even living organisms. Much remains to be discovered, yet every observed supernova helps scientists better understand the life cycle of stars and the expansion of the cosmos.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main findings of a study on dust formation in core-collapse supernova ejecta and grain survival after the reverse shock.
counterfactuals.output:
The study finds that core-collapse supernovae can condense substantial dust—typically a few tenths of a solar mass—within their cooling, expanding ejecta. The dust composition depends on ejecta mixing: carbon grains form in carbon-rich zones, while silicates, alumina, and metal grains form in oxygen-rich layers. Grain sizes vary strongly with ejecta density and progenitor structure.

When the supernova remnant’s reverse shock passes through the ejecta, grains are heated and eroded by sputtering. Small grains are usually destroyed, while larger grains are more likely to survive and reach the interstellar medium. The survival fraction depends mainly on grain size, composition, ejecta structure, and ambient gas density: dense surroundings produce earlier, stronger reverse-shock processing and greater destruction. Thus, supernovae may form large amounts of dust, but only a model-dependent fraction—often a few percent to a few tens of percent—ultimately survives, with large grains dominating the material delivered to the interstellar medium.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract explaining how supernovae could produce the large quantities of dust observed at high redshift, including condensation efficiencies, reverse-shock destruction, extinction curves, and infrared emission.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract—**The presence of \(10^{7}\!-\!10^{9}\,M_\odot\) of dust in galaxies less than a billion years after the Big Bang challenges production by long-lived asymptotic giant branch stars and motivates a major role for core-collapse supernovae. Dust can condense rapidly in cooling, metal-rich ejecta, with observations and models indicating initial yields of approximately \(0.1\!-\!1\,M_\odot\) per event, corresponding to condensation efficiencies of roughly 10–50% of available refractory material, although values depend strongly on ejecta chemistry, mixing, clumping, and grain size. The inward-propagating reverse shock subsequently sputters and fragments newly formed grains; commonly predicted survival fractions range from a few percent to several tens of percent, with larger grains and dense clumps surviving most effectively. Supernovae may therefore supply both stellar dust seeds and, under favorable conditions, substantial surviving dust masses, while rapid grain growth in the dense interstellar medium may still be required to explain the most dust-rich high-redshift systems. Supernova-condensed grains can produce distinctive ultraviolet–optical extinction curves, potentially including relatively flat or steep far-ultraviolet behavior and weak spectral features, but these signatures are not unique because later processing alters the grain-size distribution and composition. Absorbed starlight and shock energy are reradiated in the infrared: warm ejecta dust emits at mid-infrared wavelengths, whereas surviving and interstellar dust produces cold far-infrared/submillimeter emission observable from high-redshift galaxies. Joint constraints from extinction, infrared spectral energy distributions, dust temperatures, and supernova-remnant observations are thus essential for determining whether supernova production, reverse-shock survival, and subsequent interstellar grain growth can account for the early Universe’s large dust reservoirs.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the results of revisiting the Todini & Ferrara (2001) supernova dust model for 12–40 solar-mass progenitors and tracking the subsequent evolution of grains in supernova remnants.
counterfactuals.output:
Revisiting the Todini & Ferrara model with updated nucleation chemistry—particularly CO and SiO formation—showed that core-collapse supernovae with 12–40 M⊙ progenitors can initially condense roughly **0.1–0.6 M⊙ of dust**. The exact yield and composition depend on progenitor mass, metallicity, and explosion energy; the grains are mainly amorphous carbon, silicates, magnetite, and alumina.

Following the grains through the supernova-remnant phase substantially changes this picture:

- The reverse shock decelerates grains through gas drag and erodes them by thermal and kinetic sputtering.
- Small grains are preferentially destroyed, shifting the size distribution toward larger radii.
- Survival is strongly controlled by the ambient gas density: only about **2–20% of the freshly formed dust** survives, with the highest survival in low-density environments.
- Thus, the effective dust injection into the interstellar medium is generally only about **10⁻²–10⁻¹ M⊙ per supernova**, despite much larger initial condensation masses.

The study therefore supported supernovae as important early dust sources, but concluded that reverse-shock destruction sharply reduces their net contribution. Explaining the very large dust masses in high-redshift galaxies likely requires favorable low-density conditions, unusually efficient supernova production, and/or subsequent grain growth in the interstellar medium.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: How much dust forms in core-collapse supernova ejecta, what fraction survives reverse-shock sputtering, and are the surviving grains consistent with observations of a reddened quasar at z = 6.2?
counterfactuals.output:
Core-collapse supernova dust models predict that:

- **Dust initially condensed in the ejecta:** about **0.1–0.6 \(M_\odot\)** per SN for progenitors of roughly \(12–40\,M_\odot\).
- **Survival through the reverse shock:** only about **2–20%**, depending strongly on the circumstellar/interstellar gas density and grain size/composition. This leaves approximately **\(10^{-3}–10^{-1}\,M_\odot\)** of dust per event; small grains are preferentially sputtered.
- **Comparison with the \(z=6.2\) quasar SDSS J1048+4637:** **yes**. The extinction curve produced by the surviving, reverse-shock-processed grain population—particularly when averaged over a stellar initial-mass function—is broadly consistent with the quasar’s unusual reddening curve. Reverse-shock destruction actually improves the agreement by removing many small grains and flattening the extinction curve.

These values are model-dependent, especially on ambient density, ejecta mixing, and grain-size distributions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a concise research-style overview of theoretical supernova dust production, addressing the tension with observed condensation efficiencies, the influence of ambient ISM density, grain-size evolution, stochastic heating, and cold dust in remnants.
counterfactuals.output:
### Theoretical supernova dust production

Core-collapse supernova ejecta are metal-rich and can condense dust as they cool, typically within a few hundred to several thousand days. Classical nucleation and kinetic models predict initial dust yields of roughly \(0.1\!-\!1\,M_\odot\), depending on progenitor mass, ejecta mixing, molecular chemistry, and clumping. These yields correspond to large condensation efficiencies—often tens of percent of available refractory elements. Early-time infrared observations, however, commonly infer only \(10^{-5}\!-\!10^{-2}\,M_\odot\) of warm dust. This apparent tension can reflect inefficient nucleation, optically thick or clumpy ejecta, continued grain growth over decades, and the failure of mid-infrared measurements to detect colder material. Far-infrared/submillimetre observations of SN 1987A, Cas A, and the Crab reveal \(0.1\)-to-several-\(0.1\,M_\odot\) of cold dust, narrowing—but not eliminating—the discrepancy.

### Reverse shocks and ambient density

The relevant yield for galactic dust budgets is not the condensed mass but the mass surviving passage through the reverse shock. The circumstellar/interstellar density controls reverse-shock timing and strength. In denser environments, the remnant decelerates rapidly, driving an earlier reverse shock and generally increasing sputtering and grain–gas collisions; survival fractions can fall from tens of percent to only a few percent. Low-density surroundings delay processing and favor survival. Ejecta clumps complicate this trend: they can shield grains and permit rapid post-shock cooling, although transmitted shocks, grain–grain collisions, and subsequent escape from disrupted clumps may still destroy dust.

### Grain-size evolution

Survival is strongly size-dependent. Small grains have large surface-to-volume ratios and are preferentially removed by thermal and non-thermal sputtering, while grains larger than approximately \(0.05\!-\!0.1\,\mu{\rm m}\) are more likely to survive. Coagulation and accretion in dense ejecta can shift the distribution toward larger sizes; conversely, shock-driven shattering can create small fragments that are then rapidly sputtered. Consequently, remnants may inject less dust than they initially form, but with a size distribution biased toward large grains compared with the freshly condensed population.

### Stochastic heating and inferred masses

Very small grains do not maintain a single equilibrium temperature. Individual photon or electron impacts produce large temperature excursions, generating mid-infrared emission even when the grains are cold on average. Models using only equilibrium temperatures can therefore misidentify grain sizes and compositions or overestimate the warm-dust mass. Conversely, mid-infrared faintness does not imply an absence of dust: most of the mass may reside in large, cold grains that radiate primarily at far-infrared and submillimetre wavelengths.

### Cold dust and the net supernova contribution

Cold dust detections support high intrinsic condensation efficiencies, but inferred masses remain sensitive to grain opacity, composition, temperature mixing, synchrotron subtraction, and contamination by foreground or swept-up interstellar dust. The central theoretical uncertainty is thus increasingly not whether supernovae can form substantial dust, but how much remains after reverse-shock processing. Current models allow supernovae to be important dust sources—especially in young, metal-poor galaxies—provided that condensation occurs in dense clumps, grains grow to relatively large sizes, and ambient densities are low enough to permit significant survival.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
